big: Meena and four friends each have ₹10,000 to invest. None of them knows how to pick shares. So they try something smarter: they pool the money and hand it to one professional.

lines: If we pool ₹50,000, who actually owns what? And what stops the manager from running off with it?
Two good questions. The first is about units. The second is about rules. Let us take them in order.

intro: A pool of ₹200 crore has been split into 10 crore equal slices called units.
note: The NAV is worked out once every business day. Your units stay the same. The price per unit moves.

title: Who owns what?
stops: The fund house keeps your money as its own
You own units of the pool
SEBI sets rules; assets are kept apart
alt: A shield checking four statements about a mutual fund
caps: The fund house runs the pool. It does not own it.
You own units, a share of everything the pool holds.
SEBI sets the rules and the assets are kept apart from the fund house's own money.
No return is guaranteed. The unit price moves with the market.

q: Meena puts ₹10,000 into a fund whose NAV is ₹20. Next month the NAV is ₹22. What has changed for Meena?
opts: She now holds 550 units because the fund house adds units as the NAV rises
She now holds 455 units because the higher NAV removes some of her units
She holds the same 500 units, each now worth more, so her holding is worth ₹11,000
Nothing has changed until she sells, since the NAV does not affect her holding
why: Units are only added when she invests more. A rising NAV raises the value, not the unit count.
Units are never removed because the price rises. Her count stays the same at 500 units.
Units stay fixed. Her 500 units at ₹22 are worth ₹11,000. Only the price per unit moved.
Her holding is revalued at the new NAV every day, whether or not she ever sells anything.

q: A friend worries: 'If the fund house goes bankrupt, my savings in its funds vanish.' What is the most accurate reply?
opts: No, assets are kept separate and belong to the unit holders under SEBI rules
Yes, because the fund house holds your money in its own accounts for you
Mostly yes, since the fund house must sell the pool to pay its own debts first
No, because SEBI guarantees every fund against loss in all situations
why: Assets are held separately and belong to the unit holders. The fund house only manages them.
The pool's assets are kept apart from the fund house's own money, so this does not hold.
The fund house's own debts do not claim the pool's assets, which belong to the unit holders.
SEBI sets rules and oversight. It does not guarantee against market losses in any fund.

q: Two funds each hold ₹100 crore of assets. Fund A has 5 crore units and Fund B has 10 crore units. What does this tell you?
opts: Fund A is better because it has fewer units to share between its investors
Fund B is cheaper because each of its units costs less money to buy
Fund B has lost value because its units outnumber those of Fund A
Nothing about quality: Fund A's NAV is ₹20, Fund B's ₹10, same total value
why: Unit count says nothing about quality. It only shows how the same value is sliced up.
A lower NAV is not cheaper. Each unit is a smaller slice, so you simply get more units.
Having more units does not mean losing value. It only means a smaller slice per unit.
Same value, different slicing: ₹100 crore over 5 crore units is ₹20, over 10 crore it is ₹10.

q: Rohan says, 'The fund manager picks the shares, so my money is safe from falls.' What is wrong with that?
opts: Nothing, since a professional manager can avoid every fall in the market
The manager picks holdings, but the unit price still follows those holdings
He is wrong only if the fund holds shares, since bond funds cannot fall
He is right as long as the fund house is registered with SEBI
why: No manager can avoid every fall. Skill helps choose holdings but cannot remove market risk.
The manager decides the holdings. The unit price still follows how those holdings perform.
Bond funds can also fall in value, for example when interest rates rise or a borrower fails.
Registration with SEBI shows the fund follows rules. It does not shield units from falling.

pts: A mutual fund pools many people's money and you own units of the pool.
NAV is the price of one unit, worked out every business day. Your units stay fixed, the price moves.
SEBI sets the rules, and the pool's assets are kept separate from the fund house's own money.
